back: Awareness → interest → consideration → intent → evaluation → purchase.
Customer acquisition cost = marketing costs (MC) / customers acquired (CA), for a specific campaign or time window. To be optimised; compare with CLV.
Core (underlying need – "a three-inch hole, not a drill bit"), tangible (features, styling, quality, brand, packaging), augmented (added services and features).

Physical attributes (product, design, functional features) · symbolic attributes (brand, trademark, styling, packaging, price, quality) · service attributes (repair, installation, instructions, financing, spare parts, warranties, deliveries) · legal conformity.
Opportunity identification → design → testing → introduction → life cycle management (GO/NO decisions; reposition or harvest).
Value = benefits (functional, psychological, economic) − costs (monetary, perceived risk, inconvenience). Example: Lexus.

Objective: engineering assessment, indirect survey questions, VIU. Perceptual unconstrained: focus groups, direct survey questions, importance ratings. Perceptual constrained: conjoint, benchmarking. Behavioural: choice models (MNL), data mining.
Maximum willingness to pay for a focal product given a reference product. Old cost per period = new cost per period → solve for the new price. Include all usage costs (e.g. shutdowns).

1 annual cost of the old solution (units × replacements × price + downtime) · 2 annual cost of the new one with price P · 3 set equal and solve for P · 4 compare P (VIU) with the offered price: price < VIU → buy.
Conclusions about a population from a sample: estimation and hypothesis testing. H0 = no effect, H1 = hypothesised effect.

front: Type I vs. type II error
back: Type I (α): reject H0 although true. Type II (β): keep H0 although false. Fix α (usually 5%) and minimise β.
Split testing: show version A (control) to one part of the audience and version B (challenger) to another; compare a KPI. Benefits: traffic ↑, conversion ↑, bounce rate ↓, cart abandonment ↓.

front: t-test vs. chi-square in A/B tests
back: t-test: difference between means of two groups (e.g. willingness to buy – metric). Chi-square: observed vs expected frequencies (e.g. choice yes/no – categorical); test of independence or goodness of fit.

front: When is an A/B test NOT appropriate?
back: When you do not compare two versions of the same element under random assignment – e.g. comparing different products across different customer groups (→ regression).
